newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy bourse must continue reforms despite hiccup.
newsitem.headline: Italy bourse must continue reforms despite hiccup.

text.p: Italy must continue to try and attact more foreign funds in a bid to internationalise the Milan bourse despite severe technical problems on Monday which brought share trading to a halt, analysts said on Tuesday.

The breakdown in screen-trading on the stock exchange could not have come at a worse time. Corporate Italy is in the middle of its reporting results season while bourse regulators are under attack over their handling of the Olivetti affair.

"Clearly yesterday's breakdown was a major setback in the market's international image, but this should not deflect the bourse in its move to a more Anglo-Saxon type of market," said one equity strategist at a major brokerage house in Milan.
Share traders in Milan were left completely idle on Monday after a computer systems breakdown at the bourse's headquarter in Piazza Affari knocked out the exchange for a whole day.
It was only the second time transactions had been halted for an entire day since the exchange completed its move to screen-based trading in 1994.
The bourse had seen temporary breakdowns throughout last week and, though trading was back to normal on Tuesday, it was unclear whether the computer problem had been completely fixed.

The Milan bourse is currently struggling to overcome its reputation as a clubbish market controlled by a few players, with regulations not tight enough to force companies to produce clear and detailed financial information for investors.
"There is a lot to be done to the market, but progress must be made if we are to compete effectively with London, Paris and Frankfurt for investors' cash," said one Milan-based trader.

The bourse regulator Consob has come under criticism for its role in the Olivetti affair when the shares of the troubled hi-tech company were left to trade and fell like a stone after the accuracy of its financial accounts came under question.

However, analysts say that Consob is now showing more of its teeth than when it waved through a complex merger plan called SuperGemina late last year which was seen by many as a serious abuse of minority shareholder rights.

"What is needed is a more critical approach from the investment funds especially the domestic banking funds in speaking out and demanding more financial information on companies' performance," said the Milan strategist.
The bourse itself is making positive reform moves, enacting laws allowing cross-border share trading laws and pushing ahead with its own privatisation.
It is hoped this will encourage more companies to list, to add to only around 220 listed groups at present.
Privatisation stocks such as energy group ENI, telecoms holding company STET and electricity utility ENEL are expected to boost liquidity in the Milan share market.

Last November, 15 percent of ENI was floated on the market making it Italy's largest listed company but strong interest in the stock often means that 15-20 percent of the entire daily turnover of the Milan bourse is accounted for by ENI shares.

With a second tranche of ENI due to be floated in late October a further distortion to trading is likely so the privatisation of STET due in early 1997 and ENEL set for 1997 is badly needed to restore balance to trading volumes.
